body:
What a Refrigerator Actually Does

A refrigerator maintains its interior at a temperature lower than the surrounding room by continuously removing thermal energy from the refrigerated compartment.

It does not manufacture a substance called cold. Instead, it uses electrical energy to transfer heat from its relatively cool interior to the warmer surroundings.

This is important because spontaneous heat transfer normally occurs from higher temperature to lower temperature. Moving heat in the opposite direction requires an external energy input.

A refrigerator uses energy to transfer heat from a colder region to a warmer region.

Basic Working Principle of a Household Refrigerator

Most household refrigerators use a circulating fluid called a refrigerant. The refrigerant can undergo evaporation and condensation at suitable temperatures and pressures.

The refrigeration process involves the following basic functions.

  1. Absorption of heat: In the evaporator, the cold refrigerant absorbs heat from the refrigerated compartment. The refrigerant evaporates during this process.
  2. Energy supplied by the compressor: Electrical energy drives a compressor that raises the pressure and temperature of the refrigerant vapour.
  3. Release of heat: The hot refrigerant releases heat to the surrounding air in the condenser and changes back into liquid.
  4. Return to cooling conditions: The refrigerant passes through a pressure-reducing device, allowing it to return to suitable low-temperature conditions before absorbing heat again.

This process repeats as required to maintain the selected temperature.

The important school-level principle is the repeated absorption and release of heat associated with the refrigerant's changes of state.

Why the Outside of a Refrigerator Becomes Warm

The heat removed from the refrigerator's interior must be released somewhere.

It is transferred to the surrounding room through the condenser and other warm components.

The total heat released to the room includes the heat removed from the refrigerated compartment and energy supplied to operate the refrigeration system.

Therefore, the outside of a working refrigerator can become warm even though its interior remains cold.

For the same reason, leaving a refrigerator door open cannot provide sustained net cooling of a closed room. The electrical energy consumed by the refrigerator ultimately adds heat to the room.

Refrigeration Compared with Evaporative Cooling

A refrigerator and an evaporative cooler both make use of energy transfer associated with evaporation, but they operate differently.

FeatureHousehold refrigeratorEvaporative cooler
Main purposeMaintain a refrigerated compartment below room temperatureCool air by evaporating water
Working substanceRefrigerant circulating in a closed systemWater that evaporates into passing air
Main energy inputElectricity used by compressor and associated componentsUsually electricity for a fan and water circulation
Effect on humidityDoes not normally add refrigerant vapour to room airAdds water vapour to passing air
Important conditionRequires heat rejection to the surroundingsWorks best when air is relatively dry

Meaning of Energy Efficiency

Energy efficiency describes how effectively a device converts or uses supplied energy to provide the intended useful service.

For an ordinary heating appliance, efficiency can be expressed as the fraction of supplied energy delivered as useful heating.

For example, if 100 units of energy are supplied to a heating arrangement and 60 units reach the intended material as useful heat, the heating efficiency is 60%.

The remaining energy may be transferred to unintended surroundings or used in other ways.

The same simple percentage should not automatically be applied to the cooling performance of a refrigerator. A refrigerator transfers heat rather than merely converting electrical energy into cooling.

For household comparisons, the amount of electricity consumed to provide comparable refrigeration service is an important practical measure.

Ways to Reduce Unwanted Heat Transfer

Thermal insulation reduces the energy needed to maintain a temperature difference.

In a refrigerator, insulated walls and properly sealing doors reduce the rate at which heat enters from the warmer surroundings.

Keeping the refrigerator door open unnecessarily allows warmer room air to enter and increases the cooling load.

Appropriate temperature settings and adequate ventilation around the heat-releasing components can also help avoid unnecessary electricity consumption.

These measures apply the basic principles of conduction, convection and temperature difference.

India's Bureau of Energy Efficiency and Star Labelling

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), under the Ministry of Power, Government of India, administers the Standards & Labelling programme for appliances and equipment.

The programme was launched in May 2006 to help consumers understand and compare the energy performance of appliances.

Under BEE's star-labelling system, registered products are rated on a scale from 1 star to 5 stars, with higher stars indicating greater energy efficiency under the applicable rating requirements.

As of the 3 November 2026 content cutoff, BEE's published Standards & Labelling information lists both frost-free refrigerators and direct-cool refrigerators among the appliances subject to mandatory star labelling.

For meaningful comparisons, consumers should consider the applicable rating period, appliance category, storage capacity and declared energy consumption. Refrigerator labels may express annual electricity consumption in kilowatt-hours per year (kWh/year).

A 5-star rating does not necessarily mean that a large refrigerator uses less total electricity than every smaller refrigerator with fewer stars. Ratings describe efficiency according to defined product categories and standards.

Star-rating requirements and efficiency thresholds can change over time. The 2026 programme status should therefore not be treated as a permanently fixed scientific rule.

A higher star rating generally indicates better energy efficiency under the applicable BEE rating scheme. For electricity expenditure, the declared annual energy consumption is also important, particularly when comparing appliances of different sizes.

Fuel Calorific Value and Heating Efficiency

When a fuel burns, chemical energy is released, much of it as heat.

The calorific value of a fuel is the heat energy released on complete combustion of a unit mass of that fuel.

Its commonly used school-level unit is kilojoule per kilogram (kJ/kg).

A fuel with a higher calorific value releases more heat per kilogram under the specified conditions. This does not automatically mean that every device burning that fuel will operate more efficiently.

The useful heat delivered also depends on how effectively the appliance transfers energy to the intended object and limits unwanted losses.

Thus, calorific value is a property of a fuel, while appliance efficiency describes useful performance relative to energy supplied.

Connecting the Main Concepts

Heat transfer, thermal expansion, changes of state and refrigeration are connected through the behaviour of thermal energy.

A temperature difference can cause heat to flow. The transferred energy may raise temperature, change dimensions, or produce a change of physical state.

Conduction, convection and radiation determine how heat reaches or leaves a body. Thermal insulation reduces unwanted heat exchange.

During melting and vaporisation, energy is absorbed. During freezing and condensation, energy is released. Refrigeration uses these phase-change principles together with electrical energy to transfer heat away from a cooler compartment.

Prelims focus

  • A refrigerator removes heat from its interior and releases heat to its surroundings.
  • Refrigerant absorbs heat during evaporation and releases heat during condensation.
  • Electrical energy is required to transfer heat from a colder compartment to warmer surroundings.
  • BEE's Standards & Labelling programme was launched in May 2006.
  • BEE's star-rating scale runs from 1 to 5 stars, with 5 indicating higher efficiency under the applicable scheme.
  • Trap: Calorific value measures heat released per unit mass of fuel; it is not the same as the efficiency of the appliance using that fuel.
